stances.claim: The performance hierarchy is consistent across two metrics -- Top 10 producers (Ateneo 3, USC 4, UP 2, DLSU 1) and passing-rate ranking (Ateneo 86.76%, UP 84.39%, USC 72.45%) -- meaning the same elite schools dominate both topnotchers and overall passing performance.
stances.rhetorical_move: two-metrics-converge analysis to confirm a hierarchy

stances.claim: The systemic facts are alarming: 22.07% overall passing; first-timers 32.87% pass, repeaters 11.28% pass; only 37 of 131 schools above the 22.07% threshold; 25 schools with zero passers, including two with 31 and 30 candidates each.

Something is awfully unwell about the legal education system, the law schools, the students, or the exams (or all of them), and this ~25% pass rate problem has 'bedeviled the bar exams since the 1980s.'

CJ Bersamin's Legal Education Summit, with its consultations and organizing committee under Justice Gesmundo and Dean Cordero-Tan, is a welcome reform attempt to identify common problems, update the basic law curriculum, and adopt practices that develop 'practice-ready lawyers.'

The LEB's functions, as exercised through its Memorandum Orders mandating the PhiLSAT, appear to conflict with the SC's constitutional power to 'promulgate rules concerning... admission to the practice of law' -- a conflict the SC TRO has paused but not yet resolved.

The constitutional case should be finally decided before the Summit, so reform recommendations rest on settled jurisdictional ground rather than continuing tension between RA 7662 and the Constitution.

notable_anecdotes: The two zero-passer schools that fielded 31 and 30 candidates each -- singled out without naming, the single most damning data point in the column, an arithmetic that turns aggregate statistics into individual-school accountability.

The convergence-of-rankings finding -- that the same elite schools (Ateneo, UP, USC) dominate both topnotcher production and overall passing rate -- invoked to refute any 'topnotchers come from anywhere' assumption.

The 'something must be awfully unwell about the legal education system, the law schools, the students, the exams or all of them' formulation -- a rare CJ phrasing that distributes blame across all stakeholders rather than fastening on one, modeling a diagnostic neutrality.
The chronology of LEB inertia -- RA 7662 in 1993, first appointments only in 2009 -- used to illustrate how slow institutional implementation undermines legislative intent.
Self-reference to a prior column (3/14/2019) for PhiLSAT details, suggesting the column is one entry in a continuing legal-education-reform arc.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with the good news from the 2018 bar-exam results -- the Top 10 captured by three Ateneo de Manila graduates (positions 1, 4, 5), four from the University of San Carlos (2, 3, 9, 10), two from UP (6, 7), and one from DLSU (8). The bad news: only 1,800 of 8,155 takers passed (22.07%), with first-timers at 32.87% and repeaters at 11.28%. The top schools by overall passing percentage are Ateneo de Manila (86.76%), UP (84.39%), USC (72.45%), UA&P (66.67%), Ateneo de Davao (64.52%), San Beda Manila (64.50%), UST (63.16%), AUF (55.00%), Xavier (54.90%), and PLM (50.00%) -- and the convergence of the two metrics confirms that the same elite schools dominate both topnotcher production and overall pass rates. Of 131 law schools, only 37 cleared the 22.07% threshold; 25 produced zero passers, including two schools that fielded 31 and 30 candidates without a single pass. Something, CJ writes, 'must be awfully unwell about the legal education system, the law schools, the students, the exams or all of them' -- a problem that has bedeviled the bar exams since the 1980s. He welcomes CJ Bersamin's Legal Education Summit (Manila Hotel, July 31-Aug 1, 2019), one of Bersamin's four reform projects, organized under Justice Gesmundo and UP Law Dean Cordero-Tan to update curricula and adopt practices producing 'practice-ready lawyers.' He flags the constitutional conflict between RA 7662 (1993, creating the LEB) and the SC's exclusive bar-admission rule-making power, exemplified in the LEB's PhiLSAT Memorandum Orders (Dec 29, 2016 amended in 2017 and 2018), against which the SC has issued a TRO. He hopes that case will be decided before the Summit.
